Heatwave Detection and Visualization

INMET → Gap-Filling → Indicators → Heatwaves Pipeline | sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() and sus_climate_plot_heatwaves()

Dr. Max Anjos

Thauã Menezes

20 September, 2026

Source: vignettes/ondas_de_calor.Rmd
ondas_de_calor.Rmd

Introduction

Heatwaves are among the most relevant extreme climate events for public health, especially in a context of global warming, accelerated urbanization, and increasing socio-environmental vulnerability. These events are characterized by persistent periods of abnormally elevated temperatures relative to a location’s climatological baseline, and can directly affect thermal comfort, demand for health services, and mortality and morbidity from heat-sensitive causes.

In Brazil, recent episodes of extreme heat have highlighted the need for tools capable of identifying, quantifying, and visualizing heatwaves in a standardized and reproducible way. This need is even more important in studies applied to the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS), in which the integration of meteorological data, environmental indicators, and health outcomes allows researchers to investigate risk patterns, support alert systems, and back environmental health surveillance strategies.

The climasus4r package provides an integrated pipeline that spans from downloading hourly meteorological data from INMET, through gap-filling, computing climate indicators, detecting heatwaves, and visualizing the events. In this tutorial, we present each step of this process with practical examples, highlighting not only the execution of the functions but also the climatological, epidemiological, and operational interpretation of the results.

Note on reproducibility: The whole pipeline is deterministic — given the same INMET data period and the same parameters, the results are identical across runs. Code chunks marked with eval = FALSE require an internet connection for the download step (INMET) and may take a few minutes depending on the requested period.

What is a heatwave?

There is no single, universally accepted definition of a heatwave. In general, a heatwave can be understood as a period of abnormal, intense, and persistent heat, in which the observed temperature exceeds a given reference threshold for several consecutive days. This threshold can be defined in absolute terms, as a fixed temperature, or in relative terms, as a high percentile of the historical temperature distribution of a given region.

This distinction matters because the impact of heat depends on the local climatic context. A temperature considered extreme in a city with a milder climate may be relatively common in tropical or semi-arid regions. For this reason, many studies use percentile-based thresholds, such as the 90th or 95th percentile, allowing the definition of extreme heat to be adapted to the climatology of each location.

In general, most heatwave definitions combine two main components:

  1. Temperature threshold — the temperature (or thermal comfort index) must exceed a certain critical value, typically defined as a high percentile of the historical distribution (P90, P95) or as a fixed deviation from the climatological mean.
  2. Minimum duration — the extreme condition must persist for at least N consecutive days (commonly 3 or 5 days), distinguishing sustained events from isolated spikes.

The absence of consensus is not an operational limitation: climasus4r implements the seven most widely used definitions in the literature (Table 1), enabling sensitivity analyses and inter-method comparisons.

Why compare methods? In tropical and subtropical regions such as Brazil, the INMET method — calibrated for the national climatic reality — tends to detect events that generic percentile-based methods may underestimate. On the other hand, thermal comfort indices such as UTCI and WBGT capture the physiological perception of heat more completely than air temperature alone. Comparing results across methods is good sensitivity-analysis practice.

Pipeline overview

1. sus_climate_inmet() → 2. sus_climate_fill_inmet() → 3. sus_climate_compute_indicators() → 4. sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() → 5. sus_climate_plot_heatwaves()

Each step takes the output of the previous one and adds information. The function sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() expects hourly data with standardized temperature and thermal comfort index columns — exactly what sus_climate_compute_indicators() produces.

Environment setup 

# Instalar climasus4r (GitHub) se necessário
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("MaxAnjos/climasus4r")

library(climasus4r)
library(dplyr)

Optional dependencies: The visualization functions require ggplot2, ggsci, and plotly. For interactive plots, also install htmlwidgets. The climate indicators step requires slider (sliding windows) and jsonlite.

install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggsci", "plotly", "htmlwidgets", "slider", "jsonlite"))

Step 1 — Climate data acquisition (INMET)

The INMET station network

The Brazilian National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) operates the largest network of automatic weather stations in Brazil, with coverage in every state. The data are provided as CSV files at hourly resolution and include air temperature (dry bulb, maximum, minimum), relative humidity, wind speed and direction, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.

The function sus_climate_inmet() automates the download, parsing, and standardization of these files into an analysis-ready format.

Main parameters 

# Estrutura da chamada completa
df_inmet <- sus_climate_inmet(
  years        = 2010:2023,   # Vetor de anos
  uf           = "RN",        # UF (sigla) para filtrar estações
  station_code = NULL,        # Código(s) específico(s) de estação (opcional)
  use_cache    = TRUE,        # Reutilizar arquivos já baixados
  cache_dir    = "~/.climasus4r_cache/climate",
  parallel     = TRUE,        # Download paralelo
  workers      = 4,           # Número de workers
  lang         = "pt",
  verbose      = TRUE
)
Parameter Type Description
years integer or vector Years to download (e.g., 2010:2023)
uf character State abbreviation to filter stations (e.g., "RN", "SP")
station_code character Specific INMET station code(s) (e.g., "A304")
use_cache logical If TRUE, reuses files already downloaded in cache_dir
parallel logical Enables parallel download via furrr/future
workers integer Number of workers for parallel execution

Example: Natal (RN) station

In this tutorial, we use data from the automatic weather station of Natal (INMET code A304), in Rio Grande do Norte — a Brazilian Northeastern state with a semi-arid climate and a history of intense heatwaves.

# Download de dados horários (2010–2023)
# A primeira execução pode levar alguns minutos; execuções subsequentes usam cache.
df_inmet <- sus_climate_inmet(
  years        = 2010:2023,
  station_code = "A304",   # Natal - RN
  use_cache    = TRUE,
  lang         = "pt",
  verbose      = TRUE
)

# Inspecionar estrutura
glimpse(df_inmet)

The output is a data.frame with hourly resolution and columns standardized by climasus4r:

#> Rows: ~122,640  (14 anos × 365 dias × 24 horas)
#>  Columns: ~20
#> 
#>  $ date               <POSIXct>  2010-01-01 00:00:00, 2010-01-01 01:00:00 ...
#>  $ station_code       <chr>      'A304', 'A304', ...
#>  $ station_name       <chr>      'NATAL', 'NATAL', ...
#>  $ federal_unit       <chr>      'RN', 'RN', ...
#>  $ region             <chr>      'Nordeste', 'Nordeste', ...
#>  $ latitude           <dbl>      -5.84, -5.84, ...
#>  $ longitude          <dbl>      -35.21, -35.21, ...
#>  $ tair_dry_bulb_c    <dbl>      28.4, 27.9, ...
#>  $ tair_max_c         <dbl>      29.1, 28.6, ...
#>  $ tair_min_c         <dbl>      27.8, 27.3, ...
#>  $ rh_pct             <dbl>      82.0, 84.0, ...
#>  $ wind_speed_ms      <dbl>      3.2, 2.8, ...
#>  $ precip_mm          <dbl>      0.0, 0.0, ...

Data source: The raw data are CSV files publicly provided by INMET at https://portal.inmet.gov.br/dadoshistoricos. climasus4r automatically parses each annual file, applies quality control, and standardizes the column names. No interpolation or modification of values is performed at this stage.

Step 2 — Gap-filling

The problem of gaps in hourly series

Automatic INMET stations frequently show gaps caused by transmission failures, equipment maintenance, or extreme climate events. The presence of missing values (NA) in temperature columns can prevent the computation of thermal comfort indices and compromise the percentile estimates used in heatwave detection.

The function sus_climate_fill_inmet() implements intelligent gap filling based on regression models trained on correlated meteorological covariates (air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, hour of day, seasonality). Filling is performed variable by variable and respects a maximum gap threshold (gap_percentage): if the proportion of missing values in a given series exceeds this threshold, the station is flagged as low quality and no filling is applied.

Main parameters 

df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(
  df               = df_inmet,
  target_var       = "tair_dry_bulb_c",  # Variável a preencher
  datetime_col     = NULL,     # Detectado automaticamente
  station_col      = NULL,     # Detectado automaticamente
  quality_threshold = 0.4,    # Máximo de NAs para aceitar a série (40%)
  run_evaluation   = FALSE,   # Se TRUE: avalia métricas de ajuste
  gap_percentage   = 0.2,     # Intervalo máximo de gap contínuo a preencher (20%)
  keep_features    = FALSE,   # Manter covariáveis auxiliares no output
  parallel         = TRUE,
  workers          = NULL,    # NULL = detectar automaticamente
  verbose          = TRUE,
  lang             = "pt"
)

Filling the complete dataset

In practice, we apply gap-filling to each relevant temperature and humidity variable before computing thermal comfort indicators:

# Preencher temperatura do ar (bulbo seco)
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(
  df         = df_inmet,
  target_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  lang       = "pt",
  verbose    = TRUE
)

# Preencher temperatura máxima e mínima
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "tair_max_c",  lang = "pt")
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "tair_min_c",  lang = "pt")

# Preencher umidade relativa (necessária para UTCI, WBGT, HI)
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "rh_pct",       lang = "pt")

# Verificar proporção de NAs remanescentes
df_filled |>
  summarise(
    n_total    = n(),
    na_tmax    = mean(is.na(tair_max_c)),
    na_tmin    = mean(is.na(tair_min_c)),
    na_tair    = mean(is.na(tair_dry_bulb_c)),
    na_rh      = mean(is.na(rh_pct))
  )

Good practice: Always apply sus_climate_fill_inmet() before sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(). The detection function issues a warning (cli_warn) if it finds NAs in the temperature columns, but it does not fill them automatically — that decision is left to the analyst, since different imputation strategies can influence the results.

Step 3 — Computing climate indicators

Why go beyond air temperature?

Air temperature (dry bulb) is the most widely available meteorological variable, but it is not the best proxy for human thermal stress. The human body responds to the thermal environment resulting from the combination of temperature, humidity, solar radiation, and wind speed. Thermal comfort indices integrate these four factors and allow a more realistic estimate of the physiological perception of heat.

The function sus_climate_compute_indicators() computes the main indices used in the heatwave detection methodologies implemented in climasus4r:

<div class="feature-icon">🌡️</div>
<h3>UTCI</h3>
<p><strong>Universal Thermal Climate Index.</strong> The ISO 15743 reference biometeorological model. Integrates temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation into a physiological equivalent temperature (°C).</p>
<div class="feature-icon">💧</div>
<h3>WBGT</h3>
<p><strong>Wet Bulb Globe Temperature.</strong> An operational index widely used in occupational health and sports. Combines wet-bulb temperature, black-globe temperature, and dry-bulb air temperature.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🥵</div>
<h3>HI</h3>
<p><strong>Heat Index.</strong> Apparent temperature computed from dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity. Indicates how heat is perceived by the general population.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🌿</div>
<h3>PET</h3>
<p><strong>Physiological Equivalent Temperature.</strong> The temperature of a reference environment with the same heat exchanges as the body. Frequently used in urban comfort studies.</p>

:::::::

Function call 

df_indicators <- sus_climate_compute_indicators(
  df                   = df_filled,
  indicators           = "all",      # Calcular todos os indicadores disponíveis
  region               = "auto",     # Detectar região automaticamente por metadados
  apply_validity_mask  = TRUE,       # Mascarar valores fora dos limites físicos
  verify_physics       = TRUE,       # Verificar consistência física
  keep_source_vars     = TRUE,       # Manter variáveis originais no output
  verbose              = TRUE,
  lang                 = "pt"
)

# Verificar colunas adicionadas
names(df_indicators) |> grep("utci|wbgt|hi_c|pet", x = _, value = TRUE)

After this step, the data.frame contains the additional columns needed for heatwave detection using the UTCI, WBGT, and HI methods:

New column Index Unit
utci_c UTCI °C
wbgt_c WBGT °C
hi_c Heat Index °C
pet_c PET °C
utci_c_flag_extreme Hours with UTCI > 38°C logical
wbgt_c_flag_extreme Hours with WBGT > 32°C logical
hi_c_flag_extreme Hours with HI > 51°C logical

Step 4 — Heatwave detection

The sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() function

This is the central function of the climasus4r climate module. It takes hourly data (the output of sus_climate_compute_indicators()), aggregates it to daily scale, computes seasonally-varying historical percentile thresholds (using a ±15-day sliding window around each day of the year), applies each selected detection methodology, and returns a structured list with three components.

Full signature 

hw_result <- sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(
  data           = df_indicators,   # Output de sus_climate_compute_indicators()
  method         = c("WHO", "WMO", "INMET", "EHF", "UTCI", "WBGT", "HI"),
  baseline_start = "2010-01-01",    # Início do período de referência
  baseline_end   = "2020-12-31",    # Fim do período de referência
  percentile     = 90,              # Percentil para limiares (P90 por padrão)
  min_duration   = NULL,            # NULL = usar defaults por método
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Implemented methodologies

Table 1 presents the seven implemented methodologies, including the base variable, the threshold criterion, and the default minimum duration.

Table 1 — Heatwave detection methodologies implemented in sus_climate_compute_heatwaves()

Method Base variable Threshold criterion Minimum duration Reference
WHO Daily Tmax Tmax > P90(Tmax) 3 days WMO & WHO (2015)
WMO Daily Tmax and Tmin Tmax > P90(Tmax) AND Tmin > P90(Tmin) 5 days Perkins & Alexander (2013)
INMET Daily Tmax Tmax > historical mean + 5°C 5 days INMET (2009)
EHF Daily Tmean EHF > 0 (composite formula; see below) 3 days Nairn & Fawcett (2015)
UTCI Daily UTCImax UTCImax > P90(UTCImax) 3 days Broede et al. (2012)
WBGT Daily WBGTmax WBGTmax > P90(WBGTmax) 3 days Liljegren et al. (2008)
HI Daily HImax HImax > P90(HImax) 3 days Steadman (1979)

Seasonal smoothing of percentiles: For all percentile-based methods, climasus4r uses a ±15-day sliding window around each day of the year (computed over the reference period), rather than a fixed percentile computed over the whole series. This approach, recommended by Fischer & Schär (2010), eliminates seasonal bias and ensures that the same level of relative extremeness is detected at any time of year.

Foundations of the Excess Heat Factor (EHF)

The EHF (Nairn & Fawcett, 2015) is the only method that does not use direct percentiles of the base variable. It combines two components:

EHF=EHIsig×max⁡(1,EHIacc)\text{EHF} = \text{EHI}_{sig} \times \max(1, \text{EHI}_{acc})

Where:

  • EHI_sig (significance index): T‾3−T95\bar{T}_3 - T_{95}, measures how much the mean temperature of the last 3 days exceeds the climatological 95th percentile of the mean temperature. Captures the absolute magnitude of the heat.
  • EHI_acc (acclimatization index): T‾3−T‾30\bar{T}_3 - \bar{T}_{30}, measures how much the mean temperature of the last 3 days exceeds the mean of the previous 30 days. Captures the rate of warming and the population’s acclimatization capacity.

Days with EHF > 0 are classified as heatwave days. Event intensity is classified into three categories based on the 85th percentile (EHF85) of all positive EHF values observed at the station:

  • Low Intensity Heatwave (LIHW): 0 < EHF_peak < EHF85
  • Severe (SHW): EHF85 ≤ EHF_peak < 3 × EHF85
  • Extreme (EHW): EHF_peak ≥ 3 × EHF85

INMET method: calibration for Brazil

The INMET method defines a heatwave when the daily maximum temperature exceeds the climatological mean of the maximum temperature by at least 5°C for 5 or more consecutive days (INMET, 2009). The climatological mean is computed over the reference period defined by the user (1981–2010 or 1991–2020 is recommended, depending on data availability).

This criterion is particularly suitable for the Brazilian tropical and subtropical context, where absolute temperature values are already high and the health impact is more closely associated with the deviation from the local norm than with the absolute value.

Running the detection

Example 1: air-temperature-based methods 

# Métodos que requerem apenas temperatura do ar (Tmax, Tmin, Tmean)
hw_temp <- sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(
  data           = df_indicators,
  method         = c("WHO", "WMO", "INMET", "EHF"),
  baseline_start = "2010-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2020-12-31",
  percentile     = 90,
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Example 2: all methods (including comfort indices) 

# Todos os métodos — requer colunas utci_c, wbgt_c, hi_c
hw_all <- sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(
  data           = df_indicators,
  method         = "all",          # Equivale a c("WHO","WMO","INMET","EHF","UTCI","WBGT","HI")
  baseline_start = "2010-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2020-12-31",
  percentile     = 90,
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Example 3: customizing the percentile and minimum duration 

# Critério mais conservador: P95 e mínimo de 5 dias para todos os métodos
hw_strict <- sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(
  data           = df_indicators,
  method         = c("WHO", "INMET"),
  baseline_start = "2010-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2020-12-31",
  percentile     = 95,       # Limiar mais alto → menos eventos, mais intensos
  min_duration   = 5,        # Substitui os defaults por método
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Sensitivity analysis: We recommend running the detection with different combinations of percentile (P85, P90, P95) and minimum duration (3, 5, 7 days) and comparing the number of detected events. This allows the robustness of the epidemiological results to be assessed against methodological choices.

Output structure

The function returns a named list with three components:

# Inspecionar o output
names(hw_all)
#> [1] "events"  "daily"   "summary"

$events — event table

A data.frame with one row per detected heatwave event. Each row represents a continuous episode of days with the heatwave condition active for a given method and station.

# Primeiros eventos detectados
head(hw_all$events)
Column Type Description
event_id character Unique identifier: <station>_<method>_<N>
station_code character INMET station code
method character Detection method (WHO, WMO, etc.)
start_date Date Event start date
end_date Date Event end date
duration_days integer Duration in consecutive days
temp_mean double Mean temperature over the period (method-specific variable)
temp_peak double Maximum temperature over the period
anomaly_mean double Mean anomaly (temperature - threshold)
anomaly_cumulative double Cumulative anomaly over the event
severity_index double Severity index: duration × mean anomaly
ehf_peak double Peak EHF (EHF method only; NA for others)
ehf_mean double Mean EHF during the event (EHF only)
intensity_class character Classification: Low, Severe, Extreme (EHF only)
region character Geographic region of the station
federal_unit character State (UF) of the station 
# Filtrar os 10 eventos mais severos pelo índice de severidade
hw_all$events |>
  arrange(desc(severity_index)) |>
  select(event_id, method, start_date, end_date, duration_days,
         temp_peak, anomaly_mean, severity_index) |>
  head(10)
# Contar eventos por método
hw_all$events |>
  count(method, name = "n_eventos") |>
  arrange(desc(n_eventos))

$daily — daily series with flags

The daily data.frame contains one row per station per day, with aggregated variables and logical columns (TRUE/FALSE) indicating whether that day belongs to a heatwave under each method:

# Inspecionar colunas de flags
hw_all$daily |>
  select(station_code, date_day, tmax, tmean, starts_with("hw_")) |>
  head(10)

The hw_any column is TRUE if any method detected a heatwave on that day — useful for exposure analyses without committing to a single criterion.

# Dias com onda de calor ativa por pelo menos um método
hw_all$daily |>
  filter(hw_any == TRUE) |>
  select(date_day, tmax, tmean, hw_who, hw_inmet, hw_ehf, hw_utci) |>
  head(20)
# Concordância entre métodos: proporção de dias classificados por cada um
hw_all$daily |>
  summarise(
    pct_who   = mean(hw_who,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_wmo   = mean(hw_wmo,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_inmet = mean(hw_inmet, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_ehf   = mean(hw_ehf,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_utci  = mean(hw_utci,  na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_wbgt  = mean(hw_wbgt,  na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_hi    = mean(hw_hi,    na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_any   = mean(hw_any,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

$summary — annual summary

The annual summary aggregates statistics by station, method, and year, serving as the natural entry point for temporal trend analyses:

# Resumo anual
hw_all$summary |>
  filter(method == "INMET") |>
  select(year, station_code, n_events, total_days_hw,
         mean_duration, max_duration, mean_anomaly, severity_total) |>
  arrange(desc(year))
Column Description
year Year
station_code Station code
method Detection method
n_events Number of events in the year
total_days_hw Total heatwave days in the year
mean_duration Mean event duration (days)
max_duration Duration of the longest event (days)
mean_intensity Mean temperature during events
max_intensity Peak temperature during events
mean_anomaly Mean anomaly during events
severity_total Sum of the severity indices of the year’s events

Step 5 — Heatwave visualization

The sus_climate_plot_heatwaves() function

Visualization turns the structured output of sus_climate_compute_heatwaves() into interpretable plots. The function offers four types of visualization, each answering a different analytical question:

<div class="feature-icon">📅</div>
<h3>timeline</h3>
<p>A Gantt chart showing the timing, duration, and intensity of each event. Ideal for comparing events across methods and stations.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🗓️</div>
<h3>calendar</h3>
<p>A calendar heatmap displaying the daily occurrence of heatwaves across the months. Reveals seasonal patterns and intra-annual distribution.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">⚡</div>
<h3>intensity</h3>
<p>A duration × peak-temperature scatter plot, with points colored by intensity class. Distinguishes long events from hot events.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">📈</div>
<h3>trend</h3>
<p>Grouped bars showing the number of events per year and method. Allows long-term trends in heatwave frequency to be identified.</p>

Full signature 

p <- sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result     = hw_all,          # Output de sus_climate_compute_heatwaves()
  type          = "timeline",      # "timeline" | "calendar" | "intensity" | "trend"
  station_code  = NULL,            # Filtrar por estação específica
  method        = NULL,            # Filtrar por método (ex.: "INMET", "EHF")
  year          = NULL,            # Filtrar por ano (útil para "calendar")
  interactive   = TRUE,            # TRUE = plotly; FALSE = ggplot2 estático
  color_palette = "npg",           # Paleta ggsci: "npg", "lancet", "jama", etc.
  lang          = "pt",            # "pt" | "en" | "es"
  save_plot     = NULL             # Caminho para salvar (HTML ou PNG)
)
Parameter Options Effect
type "timeline", "calendar", "intensity", "trend" Chart type
interactive TRUE (plotly), FALSE (ggplot2) Interactivity
color_palette any palette from the ggsci package Color scheme
lang "pt", "en", "es" Label language
save_plot .html or .png path Save the chart to disk

Plot 1: Timeline

The timeline chart presents each event as a horizontal segment (Gantt-style), with thickness proportional to duration and color indicating the intensity class (relevant for EHF; for other methods, all events are classified as “unknown” in the intensity legend).

# Linha do tempo de todos os eventos — todos os métodos
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "timeline",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Filtrar apenas eventos pelo método INMET
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "timeline",
  method      = "INMET",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Versão estática para publicação
p_timeline <- sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result     = hw_all,
  type          = "timeline",
  method        = c("WHO", "INMET", "EHF"),
  interactive   = FALSE,        # ggplot2 puro
  color_palette = "lancet",     # Paleta Lancet (jornais biomédicos)
  lang          = "pt",
  save_plot     = "timeline_ondas_calor.png"  # Salvar em PNG
)
print(p_timeline)

Interpretation: Longer segments indicate longer-lasting events; the thickness visually reinforces the duration. Note that the WMO method (dual threshold: Tmax AND Tmin) tends to generate fewer, longer events than WHO (Tmax only), since it requires both day and night to be exceptionally hot.

Plot 2: Calendar

The calendar displays each day of the year as a colored cell — red for heatwave days, gray for normal days. It is the most intuitive chart for communicating event seasonality to a non-technical audience.

# Calendário para um ano específico — método WHO
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "calendar",
  method      = "WHO",
  year        = 2023,
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Calendário com hw_any (qualquer método) — todos os anos
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "calendar",
  method      = NULL,          # NULL → usa hw_any (qualquer método)
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt"
)

Interpretation: Note the concentration of heatwave days in the austral summer months (December–March) in the Northeast. Years with multiple consecutive red blocks deserve special attention: in these periods, excess mortality in the SUS tends to be higher (Fiocruz, 2025).

Plot 3: Intensity vs. duration

This scatter plot places each event on the duration × peak-temperature plane. Coloring by EHF intensity class (when available) allows identification of events that combine long duration and high temperature — those with the greatest epidemiological risk.

# Intensidade EHF (com classificação Low / Severe / Extreme)
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "intensity",
  method      = "EHF",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Todos os métodos juntos (sem classificação de intensidade EHF)
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "intensity",
  method      = NULL,
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt"
)

Interpretation: Events in the upper right quadrant (long duration + high temperature) are the most dangerous from a public health standpoint. Events in the lower right quadrant (long duration + moderate temperature) can be equally dangerous for non-acclimatized populations. EHF captures this nuance through the EHI_acc (acclimatization) component, penalizing events that occur after an abnormally cold period.

Plot 4: Annual trend

The trend chart shows the number of events detected per year for each method, allowing identification of whether heatwave frequency is increasing over the analyzed period — one of the main climate change scenario projections for Brazil.

# Tendência anual — todos os métodos
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "trend",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Tendência apenas para WHO e INMET (comparação de sensibilidade)
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(
  hw_result   = hw_all,
  type        = "trend",
  method      = c("WHO", "INMET"),
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt",
  save_plot   = "tendencia_ondas_calor.png"
)

Interpretation: If the frequency trend is increasing, this is consistent with regional warming. Compare patterns across methods: the INMET method tends to be more restrictive in regions that are already hot (since it requires +5°C above the historical mean), while percentile-based methods capture relative increases even in regions where absolute temperatures are elevated year-round.

Saving plots 

# Gráfico interativo → arquivo HTML autossuficiente
sus_climate_plot_heatwaves(

Exporting events for external analysis 

# Exportar tabela de eventos para CSV
write.csv(
  hw_all$events,
  file      = "eventos_ondas_calor_A304_2010_2023.csv",
  row.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

# Exportar resumo anual
write.csv(
  hw_all$summary,
  file      = "resumo_anual_ondas_calor_A304.csv",
  row.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

Concordance analysis across methods 

# Proporção de dias classificados como onda de calor por N métodos simultaneamente
hw_all$daily |>
  mutate(
    n_methods = rowSums(
      across(c(hw_who, hw_wmo, hw_inmet, hw_ehf, hw_utci, hw_wbgt, hw_hi)),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  count(n_methods) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

Concordance analysis answers a central question in environmental epidemiology: on how many of the days classified as a heatwave is there consensus among methods? High concordance increases confidence in the results; low concordance suggests that the health impact may vary significantly depending on the criterion adopted.

General concepts and percentile framework

  • Perkins, S.E. (2015). A review on the scientific understanding of heatwaves — their measurement, driving mechanisms, and changes at the global scale. Atmospheric Research, 164–165, 242–267. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.atmosres.2015.05.009
  • Perkins, S.E. & Alexander, L.V. (2013). On the measurement of heat waves. Journal of Climate, 26(13), 4500–4517.
  • Fischer, E.M. & Schär, C. (2010). Consistent geographical patterns of changes in high-impact European heatwaves. Nature Geoscience, 3, 398–403.

WHO and WMO methods

  • WMO & WHO (2015). Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development. World Meteorological Organization, Geneva.
  • WMO (2021). Guidelines on the Definition and Monitoring of Extreme Weather and Climate Events. World Meteorological Organization.

INMET method

  • INMET — National Institute of Meteorology (2009). Normais Climatológicas do Brasil 1961–1990. Brasília: MAPA/INMET.
  • MCTI/Gov.br (2025). Heatwave reports in Brazil (online).

EHF (Excess Heat Factor)

  • Nairn, J.R. & Fawcett, R.J.B. (2015). The Excess Heat Factor: A metric for heatwave intensity and its use in classifying heatwave severity. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 12(1), 227–253. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph120100227

UTCI (Universal Thermal Climate Index)

  • Broede, P., Fiala, D., Blazejczyk, K., Holmer, I., Jendritzky, G., Kampmann, B., Tinz, B. & Havenith, G. (2012). Deriving the operational procedure for the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). International Journal of Biometeorology, 56(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00484-011-0454-1

WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature)

  • Liljegren, J.C., Carhart, R.A., Lawday, P., Tschopp, S. & Sharp, R. (2008). Modeling the wet bulb globe temperature using standard meteorological measurements. Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene, 5(10), 645–655.
  • ISO 7243:2017. Ergonomics of the thermal environment — Assessment of heat stress using the WBGT index. International Organization for Standardization.

HI (Heat Index)

  • Steadman, R.G. (1979). The assessment of sultriness. Part I: A temperature-humidity index based on human physiology and clothing science. Journal of Applied Meteorology, 18(7), 861–873.
  • Steadman, R.G. (1984). A universal scale of apparent temperature. Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology, 23(12), 1674–1687.

SUS context and Brazilian public health
